claims.text: Controlled thermal aging can induce enhanced local chemical order in 316L stainless steel.
Enhanced local chemical order in 316L promotes formation of a uniform, Cr-enriched passive oxide film.
A uniform Cr-enriched passive film minimizes micro-galvanic cell formation.
Minimizing micro-galvanic cell formation improves the corrosion resistance of 316L under chemical-processing and nuclear-coolant conditions.
As-received 316L has a homogeneous austenitic structure.
As-received 316L has a random distribution of alloying elements.
Thermal treatment can tune the degree of local chemical order.
Enhanced local chemical order produces a uniform distribution of Cr at surfaces and grain boundaries.
A more uniform elemental distribution can suppress selective dissolution during passivation.
Increasing local chemical order minimizes elemental segregation at microstructural defects.
Uniform elemental distribution enables rapid repair and maintenance of a Cr-rich passive film.
Improved passive-film repair reduces pitting and localized corrosion.
Aged 316L with enhanced local chemical order will have lower corrosion-current density than as-received 316L.
Aged 316L with enhanced local chemical order will exhibit delayed pitting initiation and higher breakdown potentials than as-received 316L.
The passive layer on aged samples will be more homogeneously enriched in Cr than that on as-received samples.
The proposed effect should hold only when aging enhances local chemical order without causing carbide, sigma-phase, or other unwanted phase formation.
Elevated-temperature treatment can cause segregation, nanoclustering, or phase-related microstructural changes that confound attribution to local chemical order.
The quantitative relationship between local chemical order and passive-film quality in 316L is not established.
